text:
The air in the studio was thick with the scent of turpentine and stale coffee, a sharp contrast to the sterile, lemon-scented order of the family’s accounting firm. Liam stood before the canvas, his brush hovering over a swirl of crimson, but his hand trembled. It wasn’t fatigue; it was the weight of the letter in his pocket. His father, Arthur, had not just asked; he had demanded. The quarterly reports were due, and the senior partner position—Arthur’s ultimate concession to Liam’s "hobby"—was contingent on Liam’s presence at the office by Monday morning.

The conflict wasn't just about time; it was about identity. Every stroke Liam made felt like a betrayal of the man who had paid for his art school tuition, while every hour spent in the office felt like a slow suffocation of his soul. The tension peaked when Arthur arrived unannounced, not to discuss business, but to inspect the "mess" Liam had made of the living room, which doubled as his studio.

"You’re wasting your life on fantasies," Arthur said, his voice cold, cutting through the silence like a scalpel. He picked up a palette knife, examining the dried paint with disdain. "This isn’t a career. It’s a distraction. I built this company so you wouldn’t have to struggle. So you could have stability."

"And what if stability tastes like ash?" Liam shot back, his voice rising, cracking under the strain. He grabbed the palette knife from his father’s hand, the metal cold against his skin. "You want me to be you. But I’m not you. I’m the one who sees the world in colors you can’t even name."

The rift widened in that moment, not with a shout, but with a chilling silence. Arthur’s eyes hardened, not with anger, but with a terrifying disappointment. He didn’t yell. He simply turned and walked out, leaving the door ajar—a symbolic breach in the foundation of their relationship. Liam was left alone with the canvas, the crimson swirl now looking less like passion and more like a wound. The pressure to choose was no longer abstract; it was a physical weight pressing against his chest, forcing him to decide whether to paint his own life or inherit someone else’s.
